state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were playing with blocks of different sizes and colors. If you cut all the blocks in half or added the same amount to each block, would the overall range of sizes and colors change?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think if I cut the blocks in half, the biggest and smallest blocks would still be the same distance apart, so maybe the range wouldn't change like Tom said. But if I added the same amount to each block, wouldn't that change how far apart they are? I'm still confused about how that works. Can you explain it a bit more?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you had a set of toy cars of different sizes. If you cut all the cars in half, would the range of sizes change? And if you added the same amount to each car, would the range stay the same? Think about how the distance between the smallest and largest car would be affected in each scenario.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses vague analogies that fail to address the specific misconception, provides mathematically incorrect guidance (cutting in half does change the range), and the student remains confused and actually moves toward incorrect reasoning by Turn 2.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (blocks of different sizes and colors, toy cars) to help the student visualize and understand the abstract mathematical concept of range, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
